title: Water Cost Exposure Score
subtitle: Scores how exposed your planned hotel, senior living or multifamily building is to 20 years of rising water and sewer rates, before the plumbing is drawn.

questions.text: What annual water and sewer rate increase sits in the proforma for this building today?

answers.label: We carry today's rate flat for the whole hold period
We use a general inflation figure, around 2 to 3%
We use 4% a year because that's the number everyone uses
We use the utility's published plan for the next few years, then 4%
We run 4%, 6%, 8% and 10% side by side and set the base case from the local rate plan

questions.text: How well do you know the rate plan of the utility serving this site?

answers.label: I don't know which utility sets the sewer rate here
I know the current rate and nothing past this year
I've seen a headline about increases but haven't read the plan
I have the utility's multi-year rate plan in the project file
I have the rate plan and the capital program behind it, and I know what's funding the next increase

questions.text: What is this building's modeled water and sewer bill in its first full year of operation?
questions.hint: Use the combined water and sewer number from your proforma. If nobody on the team has modeled it yet, enter 0, and this question scores zero.

questions.text: What annual water and sewer increase would you plan on for this site over the next 20 years?
questions.hint: Recent rate programs run about 5.5% in Denver, 6% in New York, 7 to 8% in Austin, 13% in Phoenix and up to 18% proposed in St. Louis. 8% or higher scores full marks here.

low.headline: Your proforma is carrying a flat water rate
low.text: I used 4% a year in my own 20-year projections for a long time, and I now think that was too low. At 4% your water and sewer bill is 2.19 times today's number in 20 years. At 8% it's 4.66 times. If this building is modeled flat, the gap shows up in your NOI somewhere around year eight and nobody on the team will have a line for it.
steps: Pull the multi-year rate plan for the utility serving this site
Rerun the proforma at 4%, 6%, 8% and 10% water and sewer escalation
Put the 20-year water and sewer number in front of your lender before design development closes

mid.headline: You model an increase, at one rate
mid.text: You model an increase, which puts you ahead of a flat proforma. The weak spot is the single rate. Denver is running around 5.5%, Charlotte about 6.5% for commercial and multifamily, and Phoenix has seen increases reach 13%. Between 4% and 10% a year, your bill in 20 years lands anywhere from 2.19 to 6.73 times today's number, and your proforma only shows one of those outcomes.
steps: Model water and sewer escalation at three rates in the same proforma
Tie the base case to the local utility's published plan
Mark the year each scenario doubles your first-year bill

high.headline: You underwrite water the way you underwrite energy
high.text: You already treat water and sewer as a cost that climbs every year and needs a plan. The next question is how much of that exposure you remove at the building level. Greywater recycling can cut potable demand by about 35 to 50% and wastewater by a similar amount, which takes that same share off the bills you just modeled.
steps: Run your escalation scenarios with and without onsite reuse
Show the lender avoided 20-year water and sewer cost as its own line
Revisit the rate plan each time the utility files a new increase

questions.text: How were the toilets and urinals in this building specified?

answers.label: Whatever the plumbing engineer's standard spec is
Standard 1.6 gallon (6 litre) toilets across the building
High-efficiency fixtures, chosen mainly to hit a LEED or code number
High-efficiency fixtures, with flush volume modeled against occupancy
High-efficiency fixtures on a separate non-potable supply line, ready for recycled water

questions.text: What does the drain design do with shower, bath and laundry water?

answers.label: We haven't looked at drain layout past code minimums
All drains combine into one sanitary line leaving the building
The engineer knows greywater separation exists, but it isn't drawn
Shower, bath and laundry drains are separated on the drawings in some zones
Shower, bath and laundry drains are separated building-wide and routed to a planned treatment room

questions.text: Do you know this building's daily water use per occupied room, resident or unit?

answers.label: No, we size it off the code tables and move on
We have a rough number from a past project
We use a published benchmark for our building type, like 209 gallons per occupied hotel room
We have a benchmark broken out by showers, toilets, laundry, irrigation and cooling
We have an end-use model for this building, checked against a similar operating property

low.headline: Your toilets are running on drinking water
low.text: A low-flow toilet still uses 1.6 gallons, about 6 litres, of treated drinking water per flush, and each person flushes about 5 times a day. In a hotel or senior living building that's a big share of demand you pay for twice, once coming in and again as sewer. With the plumbing as drawn, you can't change that later without opening walls.
steps: Ask your plumbing engineer for a separate non-potable supply line to toilets and urinals
Separate shower, bath and laundry drains on the drawings
Get an end-use water estimate for this building type

mid.headline: Efficient fixtures on a single potable supply
mid.text: You picked efficient fixtures, which lowers the starting bill. Your exposure to rate increases keeps the same shape, because every litre is still potable and every litre still leaves as sewer. The cheapest time to add a second supply line and separate the drains is before the plumbing drawings are issued.
steps: Add a non-potable toilet supply line to the current drawings
Route greywater drains toward one mechanical room
Check the fixture model against your occupancy numbers

high.headline: Your plumbing is ready for recycled water
high.text: Separated drains and a non-potable toilet line are the hardest pieces to add after construction, and you've already designed them in. What's left is sizing treatment and storage to the flows you modeled.
steps: Size a greywater treatment system to your shower, bath and laundry flows
Match recycled water supply to toilet, irrigation and cooling demand
Document the separated plumbing for the LEED v5 Water Reuse credit

questions.text: How will water be metered in this building?

answers.label: One master meter at the street
A master meter plus a separate irrigation meter
Submeters planned for some units or zones
Submeters on every unit or wing, read monthly
Submeters on every unit plus separate meters on laundry, kitchen, cooling and any reuse system, read in near real time

questions.text: How fast would your team find a running toilet or a stuck irrigation valve?

answers.label: When the quarterly bill arrives
When the monthly bill looks off
When a guest, resident or staff member reports it
Within a few days, from submeter reads
The same day, from flow alerts

questions.text: Does your team split the water charge from the sewer charge when you model operating cost?

answers.label: We model one utility line and don't separate them
We know sewer is billed off water use but haven't modeled it separately
We model them separately at today's rates
We model them separately, each with its own escalation
We model them separately and know whether sewer here is billed on metered discharge or on water coming in

low.headline: With one meter, you find out from the bill
low.text: With a single master meter you learn about a leak, a stuck valve or a rate change a month or a quarter after it started. You also can't show a lender or a buyer where the water goes, so any water savings you claim later is hard to prove.
steps: Add submeters to units, laundry, kitchen and cooling in the current design
Split water and sewer into separate lines in the operating model
Confirm how this utility bills sewer, on metered discharge or on water coming in

mid.headline: You can see water use, a month late
mid.text: You have submeters, so the data exists. With monthly reads, a running toilet in a senior living wing can run for weeks before anyone looks. With faster reads your team catches leaks in days, and you have the baseline you'll need to measure any reuse system you add.
steps: Specify flow alerts on submeters for toilets and irrigation
Meter reuse system supply separately from potable supply
Set a daily use target per occupied room or resident

high.headline: You'll know where every litre goes
high.text: With separate meters on each end use and on reuse supply, you have proof. When rates go up you'll know the exact share of the bill you avoided, and you can show that number to an owner, a lender or a buyer.
steps: Report avoided water and sewer cost monthly alongside NOI
Compare metered daily use against the design benchmark each quarter
Share reuse volumes with the municipality when capacity questions come up

questions.text: Where is water reuse in this project's timeline?

answers.label: It hasn't come up
Someone raised it and we parked it on cost
It's on the list for a later phase or retrofit
A reuse supplier has reviewed the drawings during design development
Reuse is in the design, sized, with a mechanical room and a 20-year cost model behind it

questions.text: Which non-potable water sources have you checked for this site?

answers.label: None
Rainwater, informally
Rainwater or greywater, with a rough yield number for one of them
Greywater from showers, baths and laundry plus rainwater, with yield numbers for both
Greywater and rainwater with yields matched to toilet, irrigation and cooling demand

questions.text: How do you weigh the capital cost of a reuse system?

answers.label: As an added cost that has to come out of the budget somewhere
Against first-year water savings only
Against a simple payback at today's rates
Against 20 years of avoided water and sewer charges at one escalation rate
Against 20 years of avoided charges at several escalation rates, plus NOI, LEED v5 water credits and municipal capacity

questions.text: What share of this building's water and sewer bill does your current design remove through onsite reuse?
questions.hint: Commercially certified greywater recycling typically cuts potable demand by about 35 to 50%, with wastewater down by a similar amount. Enter 0 if reuse isn't in the design. 35% or more scores full marks here.

low.headline: This building will run 100% on potable water for 20 years
low.text: Right now every drop this building uses comes from the municipal system and goes back into it as sewer, at whatever rate the utility sets in year 5, 10 and 15. Greywater recycling can cut potable demand by about 35 to 50%, and it costs far less to design in than to retrofit. I run a complimentary water cost analysis for new builds, so send me the building type and room or unit count and I'll model it.
steps: Get a greywater and rainwater yield estimate for this site
Price reuse against 20 years of avoided water and sewer charges
Reserve space for a treatment and storage room in the current plan

mid.headline: Reuse is on the table, parked on capital cost
mid.text: You've looked at reuse and it's waiting on a budget call. If you compare the capital cost only against year-one savings, you'll pass on it almost every time. Run it against 20 years of rates at 6% or 8% and the payback gets shorter every year rates rise. I've seen 200-room hotel numbers in the $40K to $120K a year range with a 4 to 6 year payback.
steps: Model reuse capital cost against avoided charges at 4%, 6% and 8%
Bring a reuse supplier into design development
Check which LEED v5 water credits the system earns

high.headline: You've designed rising rates out of part of your bill
high.text: With reuse sized and in the design, you've removed a real share of your water and sewer exposure for the life of the building. You also free up municipal capacity the community can use for the next project, which matters more every year to the planners approving growth.
steps: Commission the reuse system with metered potable and recycled supply
Put avoided water and sewer cost into your NOI reporting
Share the demand reduction with the municipality during approvals

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.
